Foundries and Fabs

TSMC's six largest plants are all in Taiwan. In 2025 they could make more than 13 million wafers a year, out of more than 17 million for the whole company.

Foundries and Fabs, stage 9 of 15Next stage: 10 Memory and HBM

ConcentrationExtremeHigh

In plain terms

A foundry is a company that makes chips for other companies in its chip factories, or fabs. Those companies send in their designs, and the foundry runs them all through the same building on the same tools. The building costs tens of billions of dollars, and the air inside is cleaner than in an operating room. Even so, each wafer, the silicon disc the chips are built on, moves from machine to machine inside sealed boxes and never touches that air. No chip company sells enough of one product to fill such a factory on its own, so chip companies share a handful of them. TSMC runs the biggest, and all six of its largest plants are in Taiwan, so a political crisis over Taiwan would affect the whole chip supply.

In short

In 2022 Taiwan held 69 percent of the world's capacity for advanced logic chips, those below 10 nanometers, and the United States almost none[1]. In July 2026 TSMC raised its planned investment in Arizona to $265 billion across 12 facilities[2].

The industry association SEMI projected in 2026 that China would keep the world's largest installed fab capacity in 2026 and 2027[3]. China's SMIC cannot buy an EUV scanner, the machine that prints the finest layers, yet it makes 7 nm-class chips by printing those layers in several passes on older deep-ultraviolet scanners[4].

Why substitution is slow
In March 2026 SIA put the cost to build and equip a leading-edge fab at as much as $20 to $25 billion[12]. SemiAnalysis judged in December 2025 that finding the highly skilled engineers a foundry needs remained a major challenge for TSMC in Arizona[13].
Where China stands

Georgetown University's CSET reported in June 2024 that Huawei's Ascend 910B AI chip is believed to be made on SMIC's 7 nm-class N+2 process[14]. But SemiAnalysis judged in April 2025 that most 910B and 910C chips were made at TSMC[15].

Where the US stands

The US government agreed in August 2025 to buy a passive 9.9 percent stake in Intel[16]. Announcing the deal, Intel called itself the only chipmaker that both develops and manufactures leading-edge logic chips in the United States[16]. Intel Foundry lost $2.089 billion in the second quarter of 2026[17].

Specimen · wafer carrier (FOUP)

A FOUP, the sealed pod that carries 25 wafers between tools, drawn to scale. The 300 mm wafers inside, each the width of a dinner plate, nearly fill it. The shell is translucent, as the real polycarbonate is. One wafer is picked out in silver.

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

TSMC calls a plant a GIGAFAB once it can run more than 100,000 wafers a month, each a 300 mm disc, twelve inches across[18]. It operates six of them, and every one is in Taiwan[5].

How it works

Inside, a chip is built up in layers, and a similar loop of steps repeats for each one. Wafers travel in batches, called lots, inside a sealed pod called a FOUP, short for front-opening unified pod. Entegris, a US maker of these pods, offers a standard version that holds 25 wafers[19]. An overhead track carries the pod from tool to tool.

At each tool a robot lifts one wafer out and the tool does its one job, such as depositing a film, printing a pattern, etching it, cleaning it or measuring it. Then the robot puts the wafer back. The pod moves on to the next tool, often across the building. When a layer is finished, the loop starts again with the next one.

Turning silicon into a finished, packaged chip takes 1,000 to 1,500 steps, depending on how complex the chip is, the Semiconductor Industry Association said in 2025[20]. In 2021 the association put the time to make a finished wafer at about 12 weeks on average, and up to 14 to 20 weeks for advanced processes[21].

The pod keeps the wafer clean for all of that time because the wafer never meets the room's air. Intel said in 2018 that the air in its fab cleanrooms is filtered to 1,000 times fewer airborne particles than a sterile hospital operating room[22].

Every design in the building runs on the same tools because each tool is set by a recipe, the list of gases, temperatures and times for one step. A foundry offers each customer the same list of recipes on shared machines. The tools run day and night, because an idle tool earns nothing. The finished wafer is tested (see Test and assembly), then cut and packaged.

TSMC, founded in 1987, pioneered the pure-play model, in which a foundry makes only its customers' products[23]. In 2023 the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) estimated that a new fab for chips at 2 nm and below, completed in 2026, would cost $35 to $43 billion to own over ten years[6]. That is 33 to 66 percent above 2023 costs[6]. In March 2026 the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) told the US Senate that building and equipping a leading-edge fab takes as much as $20 to $25 billion of capital[12].

Together, the plants TSMC and its subsidiaries run had capacity for more than 17 million wafers a year in 2025, counted as if each were the standard 12-inch size[5]. The six largest plants, called gigafabs, had a combined capacity of more than 13 million[18]. The other plants are five smaller fabs in Taiwan, two in China, two in the United States and one in Japan[5].

Variants and trade-offs

Pure-play foundries

TSMC and UMC, both based in Taiwan, make chips only for other companies. Chips at 7 nm and below, meaning the newest processes, were 79 percent of TSMC's wafer revenue in the third quarter of 2026[7]. That share split into 33 percent at 3 nm, 28 at 5 nm, 10 at 7 nm and 8 at 2 nm[7]. TSMC's revenue for the quarter was $46.72 billion, at a 66.4 percent gross margin[7].

Integrated device makers turned foundry

Intel and Samsung design and sell their own chips and rent out capacity too. Renting out capacity is harder for them, because customers dislike handing designs to a competitor and the company's own products take the best capacity. Intel Foundry reported $5.8 billion of segment revenue in the second quarter of 2026 and an operating loss of $2.089 billion[17]. Only $293 million of that revenue came from outside customers[8]. Intel says substantially all of its foundry business still makes Intel's own products[8].

National champions

China's SMIC and Hua Hong and Japan's Rapidus have government backing. SMIC's revenue rose 16.2 percent to $9.327 billion in 2025, at a 21 percent gross margin[10]. Its lines ran 93.5 percent full, on monthly capacity above a million wafers counted in the smaller 8-inch size[10]. SMIC cannot buy an EUV scanner, yet it makes 7 nm-class chips on its N+2 and N+3 processes by printing the tightest layers in several passes on older deep-ultraviolet scanners[4].

Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) reported in June 2024 that Huawei's Ascend 910B AI chip is believed to be made on N+2[14]. It also reported that SMIC's limited 7 nm capacity forced Huawei to choose between its most advanced phone chips and its AI chips[14]. But the research firm SemiAnalysis judged in April 2025 that most 910B and 910C chips were made on TSMC's 7 nm process, from wafers Huawei bought through another company[15].

In February 2026 Rapidus raised 267.6 billion yen from the Japanese government and 32 companies to reach 2 nm mass production by 2027[11].

Mature-node capacity

Most wafers come off older lines. These make power devices, analog chips and microcontrollers, and they compete on price. In January 2025 the industry association SEMI forecast that foundry capacity at all nodes would rise from 11.3 million wafers a month in 2024 to a record 12.6 million in 2025, counted in the 8-inch size[24]. Its June 2024 forecast had credited much of that growth to Intel's new foundry business and China's expansion[25]. But in July 2025 Intel scaled back its own expansion plans, saying it would no longer go ahead with planned projects in Germany and Poland and would slow construction in Ohio[26].

Capacity and cost

In March 2025 TSMC announced plans to add $100 billion to the $65 billion it was already investing in Phoenix, for three more fabs, two packaging plants and an R&D center[27]. In July 2026 it announced another $100 billion for four more fabs at 2 nm or below, taking its planned investment in Arizona to $265 billion across 12 facilities[2].

Some customers pay TSMC in advance to hold capacity at its fabs[28]. These deposits stood at NT$189,858.2 million at the end of 2025, down from NT$291,101.8 million a year earlier[28]. Epoch AI estimated that in 2025 the four largest AI chip designers used around 90 percent of the world's CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM memory supply, against only 12 percent of advanced logic production[29]. See Advanced packaging.

Who makes it

In August 2025 the US government agreed to buy 433.3 million newly issued Intel shares at $20.47 each, or $8.9 billion in all, for a 9.9 percent stake[16]. It would pay with $5.7 billion of CHIPS Act grants that Intel had not yet received and $3.2 billion from the Secure Enclave program[16]. Announcing the deal, Intel's chief executive, Lip-Bu Tan, called Intel the only semiconductor company that both develops and manufactures leading-edge logic chips in the United States[16]. The deal closed on 27 August 2025 and made the government one of Intel's largest stockholders, Intel said in its annual report for 2025[30].

The stake is passive, with no board seat[16]. The government agreed to vote with Intel's board on matters that need shareholder approval, with limited exceptions[16]. The deal also gave the government a five-year warrant, a right to buy a further 5 percent of Intel at $20 a share[16]. The government can use that right only if Intel's ownership of its foundry business falls below 51 percent[16].

In 2026 Intel began high-volume manufacturing of some of its Panther Lake processors using ASML's High-NA extreme ultraviolet scanners[17]. It also put its 18A-P process into risk production, the trial runs a process goes through before it is signed off[17].

In 2022 Samsung broke ground in Taylor, Texas, on a plant with an initial minimum investment of $17 billion, split into $6 billion for buildings and $11 billion for equipment[31]. In December 2024 the Commerce Department awarded Samsung up to $4.745 billion of CHIPS Act funding, to support more than $37 billion of planned investment in Central Texas[9]. That plan covers two new leading-edge logic fabs and a research fab in Taylor, and an expansion of Samsung's existing plant in Austin[9].

The chokepoint

In 2022 South Korea and Taiwan held almost all of the world's logic capacity below 10 nm[32]. The United States had almost no capacity below 10 nm that year[32]. In May 2024 SIA and BCG projected that the US share of that capacity would reach 28 percent by 2032[1]. They also projected that new fab investment worldwide would reach around $2.3 trillion from 2024 to 2032[33].

Across all nodes, old and new, SEMI forecast in June 2024 that China would have installed capacity of 10.1 million wafers a month in 2025, the most of any region[25]. It forecast 5.8 million for Taiwan, out of a world total of 33.7 million, all counted in the 8-inch size[25]. In the third-quarter 2026 update of its World Fab Forecast, SEMI projected that China would keep the largest installed capacity in 2026 and 2027[3]. Little of China's capacity is advanced[34].

Chip production in Taiwan faces three risks:

  • Seismic. Taiwan sits on an active plate boundary, and after an earthquake in January 2025 TSMC had to scrap some wafers in process[35].
  • Power. A gigafab is a large industrial load on a small island grid.
  • Political. Taiwan held 69 percent of the world's logic capacity below 10 nm in 2022[1]. In December 2025 SemiAnalysis put Taiwan's share of the world's advanced-node capacity at over 90 percent, though it did not say which node sizes count as advanced[13]. So a blockade or conflict would cut most of that output off from the world market at once. See Who Controls the Chain.

Building capacity outside Taiwan is slow, and TSMC has yet to build a gigafab anywhere else[5]. SemiAnalysis wrote in December 2025 that a foundry needs highly skilled engineers to get the most working chips from each wafer[13]. It judged that finding enough workers remained a major challenge for TSMC in Arizona[13].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What is a foundry?

A company that makes chips designed by other companies.

A chip factory, or fab, costs tens of billions of dollars, and no chip company sells enough of one product to fill a fab by itself. Reread: How it works

Where are TSMC's largest plants?

All six are in Taiwan.

In 2025 they could make more than 13 million wafers a year, out of more than 17 million for the whole company. Reread: How it works

What did SemiAnalysis judge in December 2025 to be a major challenge for TSMC in Arizona?

Finding enough skilled workers.

A foundry needs highly skilled engineers to get the most working chips from each wafer. TSMC's planned investment in Arizona reached $265 billion in July 2026, but all six of its largest plants are still in Taiwan. Reread: The chokepoint

How much of China's fab capacity can make the newest chips?

Little of it.

In its third-quarter 2026 World Fab Forecast, SEMI projected that China would keep the world's largest installed fab capacity in 2026 and 2027. SMIC cannot buy an EUV machine, so it makes its 7 nm-class chips by building the tightest layers in several patterning steps. Reread: The chokepoint
